lesson.title: Solving AC Circuits Without Calculus: Phasors, Impedance, and Kirchhoff's Laws Together
lesson.summary: AC circuit analysis converts sinusoidal sources into phasors and circuit elements into impedances, which lets Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws apply exactly as they do in DC, only now with complex numbers.
lesson.body:
Every inductor and capacitor in a circuit contributes a derivative term, L di/dt or C dv/dt, to the differential equation that governs it, and solving a fresh differential equation for every new circuit configuration gets old fast. The phasor technique sidesteps this entirely for steady-state sinusoidal signals of a single frequency. If a voltage or current is v(t) = Vm cos(wt + theta), we can represent it instead by the complex number V = Vm at angle theta, a phasor, and it turns out that taking a time derivative corresponds exactly to multiplying the phasor by jw. A differential equation in time becomes a plain algebraic equation in complex numbers, no calculus required once the setup is done.

Once every source is written as a phasor and every resistor, inductor, and capacitor is written as its impedance, R stays R, an inductor becomes jwL, a capacitor becomes 1/(jwC), which is the same as -j/(wC), the circuit looks exactly like a DC resistive circuit, just with complex numbers everywhere instead of real ones. That means Kirchhoff's voltage law, the sum of voltage phasor drops around any closed loop equals zero, and Kirchhoff's current law, the sum of current phasors into any node equals zero, both hold in this phasor form without modification. Series and parallel combination rules, voltage dividers, current dividers, even Thevenin and Norton equivalents, all carry over directly.

Apply this to a series RC circuit driven by v(t) = 100 cos(1000t) V, with R = 100 ohms and C = 10 microfarads. The source phasor is V = 100 at angle 0 degrees V, using peak amplitude here, so the resulting current will also be a peak-amplitude phasor. The capacitor's reactance at w = 1000 rad/s is XC = 1/(wC) = 1/(1000 times 10e-6) = 1/0.01 = 100 ohms, so its impedance is -j100 ohms. The total series impedance is Z = 100 - j100 ohms, with magnitude |Z| = sqrt(100^2 + 100^2) = 100*sqrt(2), about 141.4 ohms, and angle theta = arctan(-100/100) = -45 degrees. By phasor Ohm's law, the current is I = V/Z, about 0.707 A at angle 45 degrees, leading the voltage by 45 degrees, as you would expect from a capacitive circuit.

It is worth confirming KVL actually still holds with these complex numbers. The resistor voltage is VR = IR = 0.707 at 45 degrees times 100 = 70.7 V at 45 degrees, which in rectangular form is 50 + j50 V. The capacitor voltage is VC = I times (-j100) = 0.707 at 45 degrees times 100 at -90 degrees = 70.7 V at -45 degrees, or 50 - j50 V. Adding them, (50 + j50) + (50 - j50) = 100 + j0 = 100 V at 0 degrees, exactly matching the source. KVL closes perfectly, confirming that treating this AC circuit as a complex-number version of a DC circuit gives the physically correct answer, and the same confirmation would work with KCL at any node in a more complicated multi-branch circuit.
